title: Cybersecurity 100-Mark Professional Mock Examination (Test 3)

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: Which security property guarantees that sensitive payload data has NOT been altered or tampered with during transit or storage?

options.text: Usability
Integrity
Confidentiality
Availability

questions.explanation: The CIA Triad consists of Confidentiality (secrecy), Integrity (trustworthy/unaltered data via HMAC/hashes), and Availability (uptime).

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: Why must password storage use slow, salted, memory-hard hashing (Argon2id or bcrypt) instead of fast SHA-256?

options.text: General-purpose hashes like SHA-256 run at billions of guesses/second on GPUs; slow salted hashes resist brute-force and rainbow tables
SHA-256 output is reversible back to plaintext mathematically
Web frameworks crash when comparing 64-character hex strings
Argon2 hashes never require storage in databases

questions.explanation: Password hashing requires deliberately high computational & memory work factors plus per-user cryptographic salts.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in Cybersecurity

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: What is the primary difference between Encoding (e.g., Base64), Hashing (SHA-256), and Encryption (AES-256-GCM)?

options.text: Base64 protects passwords safely when transmitted over plaintext HTTP
AES-256 destroys original plaintext irreversibly
All three terms are exact cryptographic synonyms
Encoding transforms format reversibly without keys; Hashing is one-way fixed digest; Encryption provides confidentiality via secret keys

questions.explanation: Confusing encoding with encryption is a critical vulnerability—anyone can decode Base64 without credentials.

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: Which defense eliminates SQL Injection (SQLi) vulnerabilities cleanly at the root architectural level?

options.text: Encrypting the hard drive volume with BitLocker
Enabling gzip HTTP compression on API responses
Parameterized queries / prepared statements separating SQL commands from bound literal inputs
Blacklisting the uppercase word 'SELECT' via frontend regex

questions.explanation: Parameterized statements ensure the DB parser treats user inputs strictly as data values, never executable SQL grammar.

questions.prompt: In TLS (HTTPS), how do browsers verify the authenticity of a server's public key certificate?

options.text: By hashing the favicon image
By validating its cryptographic signature chain back to a trusted root Certificate Authority (CA), checking domain SAN and expiration
By calling the site owner over DNS UDP port 53
By accepting any self-signed key blindly during TLS 1.3 handshake

questions.explanation: PKI chain-of-trust validation prevents active Man-in-the-Middle impersonation attacks.

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: Which protections defend session cookies against hijacking and Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) theft?

options.text: `HttpOnly` flag blocking `document.cookie` JavaScript access
`Secure` flag ensuring transmission strictly over HTTPS
`SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` mitigating CSRF cross-origin submissions
Storing raw session IDs directly inside URL query strings

questions.explanation: Hardened session cookies combine HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite flags to shut down JS exfiltration and CSRF.

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: What security principle defines 'Defense in Depth'?

options.text: Relying strictly on a strong outer edge perimeter firewall with zero internal auth
Hiding application source files inside proprietary binary encodings
Running every internal container with full root privileges
Layering multiple independent preventive, detective, and corrective security controls so single-control failure does not lead to breach

questions.explanation: Defense in depth combines WAF, TLS, MFA, RBAC, input sanitization, network segmentation, and SIEM monitoring.

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: Which vulnerability occurs when an application modifies an authorization parameter (e.g., `/api/orders/1002` instead of `/api/orders/1001`) without verifying object ownership server-side?

options.text: ARP Spoofing
Stack Buffer Smashing
Broken Object Level Authorization (IDOR / BOLA)
DNS Cache Poisoning

questions.explanation: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference / OWASP API1 BOLA) occurs whenever backend routes fail to assert `record.ownerId === authenticatedUserId`.

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: In NIST Incident Response (SP 800-61), which phase follows 'Detection & Analysis' to stop a compromised host from spreading malware laterally?

options.text: Archiving user accounts publicly
Containment, Eradication & Recovery
Preparation only
Rebooting and deleting all audit logs

questions.explanation: NIST IR lifecycle: Preparation -> Detection & Analysis -> Containment, Eradication & Recovery -> Post-Incident Activity.

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: Which HTTP header restricts which JavaScript origins, script nonces, and frames a browser is allowed to load/execute, mitigating XSS?

options.text: Content-Security-Policy (CSP)
X-Powered-By
Cache-Control: public
Accept-Encoding: gzip

questions.explanation: Strict CSP policies block inline unsafe scripts and restrict external script hosts, providing robust secondary XSS defense.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in Cybersecurity

questions.prompt: Examine this Express/Node handler. Identify the critical security flaw enabling account takeover or unauthorized record reads:

options.text: Returning JSON breaks TLS transport encryption
Missing ownership check: `requireAuth` checks login, not whether `invoice.userId === req.auth.userId` (IDOR vulnerability)
Async handlers are unsupported in Express
GET endpoints cannot take path parameters like `:id`

questions.explanation: Authentication (Who are you?) is distinct from Authorization (Do you own invoice `:id`?). Always scope DB queries by `AND user_id = authenticatedUserId`.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in Cybersecurity

Normal browser TLS session resumption

questions.prompt: Identify why storing JWT access tokens inside `window.localStorage` increases risk compared to `HttpOnly` Secure cookies:

options.text: `localStorage` deletes all entries every 5 seconds automatically
Browsers strip `localStorage` on HTTPS origins
JWTs cannot contain JSON claims when placed inside storage
Any Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) payload or malicious third-party npm analytics script can read `localStorage` directly; `HttpOnly` cookies cannot be read by JS

questions.explanation: `HttpOnly` cookies isolate credentials completely from DOM JavaScript access.

questions.prompt: Why does `dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: userBio }}` without sanitization expose users to Stored XSS?

options.text: It sends user passwords directly to browser console
It converts JSON into XML schemas
Malicious `` or `
React automatically escapes HTML inside `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`

questions.explanation: Bypassing React's default DOM text escaping renders raw user HTML unless scrubbed strictly with a sanitizer like DOMPurify.

questions.prompt: Notice this authentication comparison: `if (providedSignature === expectedSignature)`. Why might high-precision benchmarks warn against `===` for HMAC secrets?

options.text: Strict equality throws errors on hexadecimal characters
Standard short-circuit string equality leaks comparison progress timing byte-by-byte; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual()`
Triple equals ignores string casing
HMAC signatures must be compared alphabetically via `<`

questions.explanation: Constant-time comparison (`crypto.timingSafeEqual`) mitigates cryptographic timing side-channel attacks.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in Cybersecurity

questions.prompt: During an active ransomware outbreak inside one VLAN subnet, what is the FIRST containment action after verifying compromise?

options.text: Pay ransom immediately before analyzing scope or backups
Isolate the infected hosts/VLAN via network ACL/EDR quarantine while preserving volatile memory/disk forensic evidence rather than wiping immediately
Format every server hard drive immediately destroying forensic timeline logs
Disable all logging daemons across the organization

questions.explanation: Containment stops lateral encryption/exfiltration immediately while preserving artifacts for root-cause investigation.

questions.prompt: Your public authentication endpoints receive automated credential stuffing from a distributed botnet of 10,000 rotating IPs. Blocking single IPs fails. What layered controls mitigate the attack?

options.text: Apply per-account sliding-window rate limits, breached-password screening, step-up MFA, and risk-based WAF challenges
Remove password length requirements to speed logins
Lock accounts permanently forever after 1 single mistyped character (causing attacker-triggered DoS)
Switch logins to HTTP GET query parameters

questions.explanation: Combining rate-limiting, credential-breach checks, MFA, and progressive backoff foils botnets without causing easy account lockouts.

questions.prompt: An internal microservice verifies webhook callbacks from Stripe. What stops attackers from forging fake 'payment_succeeded' requests?

options.text: Check if `User-Agent` contains the string `'Stripe'`
Allow any POST containing `"paid": true` inside JSON
Trust incoming HTTP `Origin` header alone
Cryptographically verify the signed HMAC timestamped signature header against the shared webhook secret before parsing side effects

questions.explanation: User-Agent and headers are trivially spoofed. Signed HMAC + timestamp replay tolerance guarantees webhook authenticity.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in Cybersecurity

questions.prompt: A user uploads a profile avatar image to an S3-backed portal. What upload hardening protects your backend from Remote Code Execution (RCE) and XSS?

options.text: Trust client browser `Content-Type` header blindly
Allow arbitrary `.svg` scripts executed inline on the main origin
Validate magic bytes, enforce strict size/MIME allowlist, rename files to random UUIDs, serve from an isolated domain with `Content-Disposition: attachment` or `nosniff`
Check only `file.name.endsWith('.png')` and store into `/var/www/public/uploads` executing server scripts

questions.explanation: Magic-byte validation, randomized keys, non-executable storage domains, and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` defeat file-upload exploits.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in Cybersecurity

questions.prompt: To avoid Secret Leakage in CI/CD logs and frontend bundles in Next.js, what naming/deployment rule is strictly enforced?

options.text: Commit `.env.local` into public Git history using Base64
Never prefix sensitive keys (DB service role, AI API keys, signing secrets) with `NEXT_PUBLIC_`; access them strictly on server modules
Store secret API tokens inside `localStorage` during build
Prefix all secrets with `NEXT_PUBLIC_` so SSR runs faster

questions.explanation: Any variable prefixed with `NEXT_PUBLIC_` is inlined verbatim into public browser JavaScript bundles.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in Cybersecurity

questions.prompt: Configure an iptables / firewall drop rule blocking ongoing malicious SSH brute-force traffic from `198.51.100.77` on port 22:

options.text: `iptables -I INPUT -s 198.51.100.77 -p tcp --dport 22 -j DROP`
`iptables -A INPUT -s 0.0.0.0/0 -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT`
`chmod 777 /etc/ssh/sshd_config`

questions.explanation: Inserting (`-I INPUT`) a DROP rule targeting the specific source IP and port blocks subsequent probes immediately.

questions.prompt: You discover a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) risk where users submit URLs for link previews. How must your backend fetch those URLs securely?

options.text: Allowlist HTTPS scheme only, resolve DNS first and block private/loopback/link-local CIDRs (127.0.0.0/8, 10.0.0.0/8, 169.254.169.254), and disable automatic redirects
Check only `url.startsWith('http')` before calling `fetch(url)`
Reject URLs literally containing `'localhost'` as plain text (easily bypassed via 127.1 or IPv6 `::1`)
Pass user URL directly into shell `curl`

questions.explanation: Robust SSRF defense checks the resolved IP address range against RFC 1918 / cloud metadata (`169.254.169.254`) and blocks unsafe HTTP redirects.

questions.prompt: Which `openssl` or cryptographic approach confirms an integrity-checked webhook payload in Node.js?

options.text: `Buffer.from(body).toString('base64')`
`JSON.stringify(body).length === expectedLength`
`Math.random().toString(36)`
`crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(rawBody).digest('hex')` verified via `crypto.timingSafeEqual`

questions.explanation: HMAC-SHA256 over the exact raw request body verified in constant time ensures both payload integrity and sender secret possession.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in Cybersecurity

questions.prompt: When writing audit logs for security events (logins, role changes, deletions), which practice preserves forensic trust?

options.text: Allow regular users to edit or delete their own audit log rows
Store audit logs only inside ephemeral client browser memory
Write immutable structured logs (timestamp, actorId, action, IP, status) to append-only central SIEM storage WITHOUT logging plaintext passwords or secrets
Log full raw JWTs and passwords inside `console.log` so engineers can debug faster

questions.explanation: Security logs must never record sensitive secrets/passwords and should stream to tamper-evident central logging.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in Cybersecurity

questions.prompt: An API enforces RBAC via JWT claims. Before honoring `role: 'admin'` inside the decoded payload, what MUST the server perform?

options.text: Accept unsigned JWTs when `alg: 'none'` is specified
Verify cryptographic signature (`alg` allowlisted RS256/EdDSA, NOT `none`), `exp`, `iss`, and `aud` claims via trusted server verification
Decode middle Base64 payload segment using `JSON.parse(atob(...))` directly
Read `role` from an additional hidden form field in the request body

questions.explanation: Base64 JWT payloads can be freely forged by anyone; cryptographic verification against trusted public keys/secrets is mandatory.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in Cybersecurity

questions.prompt: An enterprise migrates to Zero-Trust Network Architecture (ZTNA). How does service-to-service trust work compared to legacy castle-and-moat VPNs?

options.text: Firewall rules are disabled internally for faster RPC latency
Every workload request is mutually authenticated (mTLS) and authorized per request using short-lived identity tokens, regardless of internal subnet origin
All traffic inside `10.0.0.0/8` trusts all internal servers without encryption or authentication
Security teams share one static VPN certificate forever

questions.explanation: Zero trust assumes compromise inside any network perimeter and mandates explicit authentication, encryption, and least privilege everywhere.

questions.prompt: A SaaS platform supports multiple tenant companies sharing PostgreSQL tables. How do you enforce multi-tenant data isolation at the database engine layer itself?

options.text: Enable PostgreSQL Row-Level Security (RLS) policies binding `tenant_id` to session context alongside backend ownership checks
Hide records using CSS `display: none` in React components
Increment numeric record IDs starting at 1 per client
Disable WHERE filtering and drop unauthorized rows on the browser

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL RLS enforces strict tenant isolation directly in the DB engine as defense-in-depth alongside API authorization.

questions.prompt: During threat modeling (STRIDE) for a new file-sharing feature, how do you systematically surface vulnerabilities before writing code?

options.text: Skip design review and rely purely on an automated linter after production launch
Assume SSL/HTTPS automatically stops authorization bugs and business logic exploits
Publish raw source code publicly hoping security researchers fix bugs
Diagram trust boundaries and data flows, then evaluate Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, DoS, and Elevation of Privilege per flow

questions.explanation: STRIDE threat modeling identifies architectural trust-boundary weaknesses before costly post-launch remediation.
